metadata.scope: e_maghreb (all baronies across k_africa, k_anbiya, and k_sahara)
metadata.hierarchy_note: hierarchy reflects data/ck3_title_tree.json (save-derived de jure tree including x_script_* dynamic titles); downstream localisation/historicity mods should key on barony_key and join against their target landed_titles tree.

schema_notes.modern_name: Clean modern/vanilla English display name of the audited settlement or holding.
schema_notes.hierarchy: De jure title hierarchy from data/ck3_title_tree.json (empire, kingdom, duchy, county, holding_type).
schema_notes.first_mention_year: Integer year of earliest documented attestation (negative values = BCE; null if no pre-modern attestation was identified).
schema_notes.first_mention_attestation: Summary of the earliest documented textual or epigraphic attestation (or unattested status).
schema_notes.is_historical_867: Boolean: true iff first_mention_year is known and <= 867 CE for the audited barony name.
schema_notes.named_after_post_867_person: Boolean: true if the title name incorporates a person, saint, or dynasty post-dating 867 CE.
schema_notes.eponym_details: Explanatory text for any eponymous origin (both pre-867 and post-867 eponyms); null if not eponymous or unrecorded.
schema_notes.natural_proper_name: Object indicating whether the title derives from a hydronym, oronym, choronym, or topographic_feature.
schema_notes.morphemes: List of constituent roots/morphemes with form, language, language_code (ISO 639-3 / ISO 639-5), and English translation.
schema_notes.etymology_analysis: Linguistic and historical etymology of the audited barony name.
schema_notes.older_name_by_867: Object indicating whether a distinct older name strictly attested <= 867 CE exists for the same site or immediate predecessor.
schema_notes.source_url: Primary reference URL (typically Wikipedia or regional historical encyclopedia), or null if unavailable.

b_sfax.first_mention_attestation: Aghlabid foundation of the fortified city of Safaqis in 849 CE on the ruins of ancient Taparura.

morphemes.translation: Sfax (etymology uncertain; possibly from Berber/Punic substrate or Arabic root)

b_sfax.etymology_analysis: Arabic Safaqis (Tunisian Arabic Sfaqes), attested from the Aghlabid foundation in 849 CE. Its ultimate etymology is uncertain, with folk traditions linking it to the Numidian king Syphax or to local agricultural produce.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Pliny the Elder, Naturalis Historia (77 CE)
older_name_by_867.notes: Ancient Punic and Roman port town on the exact site of modern Sfax before the 849 CE Aghlabid refoundation.

b_el_jem.first_mention_attestation: Al-Bakri, Kitab al-Masalik wa'l-Mamalik (1068 CE), mentioning Qasr al-Jamm.

morphemes.translation: Jem (uncertain origin; medieval name for the Roman amphitheater site)

b_el_jem.etymology_analysis: Arabic al-Jamm (French El Djem), of uncertain origin, applied in the medieval period to the settlement around the Roman amphitheater of Thysdrus.

older_name_by_867.notes: Major Roman city in Africa Proconsularis/Byzacena, built on an earlier Punic settlement, famous for its 238 CE amphitheater.

b_slakta.first_mention_attestation: 2nd-century CE Ostia Piazzale delle Corporazioni mosaic (Statio 23: Navicularii Syllectini) and Antonine Itinerary (Syllectum/Sullecthum).

morphemes.translation: ancient coastal port name, adapted into Arabic as Salakta/Slakta

b_slakta.etymology_analysis: Arabic Salakta/Slakta is the direct phonological continuation of Latin Sullecthum (also Syllectum in Procopius, 533 CE), an ancient Phoenician-Punic and Roman port town.

b_bir_amir.first_mention_attestation: No pre-867 CE attestation; modern desert locality in Remada delegation, Tataouine Governorate, southern Tunisia.
b_bir_amir.eponym_details: Named after a desert well (bi'r) associated with a figure named Amir (or the title amir, 'commander/prince'); date and historical identity of the eponym are unrecorded.
b_bir_amir.etymology_analysis: Arabic compound Bi'r Amir ('Well of Amir'), designating a desert watering station and village south of Tataouine.

b_sinawin.first_mention_attestation: No pre-867 CE attestation; Saharan oasis settlement in Nalut District, northwestern Libya.

morphemes.translation: indigenous oasis toponym of uncertain etymology

b_sinawin.etymology_analysis: Berber/Amazigh oasis name Sinawin (Arabicized as Sinawan), located on the caravan route between Nalut and Ghadames.

b_ghadames.first_mention_attestation: Pliny the Elder's account of Lucius Cornelius Balbus's 19 BCE campaign, recording the Romanized form Cydamus.

morphemes.translation: Ghadames (connected to the ancient Berber tribe Tidamensi)

b_ghadames.etymology_analysis: Arabic Ghadamis derives from Latin Cydamus, itself an adaptation of the ancient Berber ethnonym/toponym Tidamensi (folk-etymologized in Arabic as ghada ams, 'lunch yesterday').

b_daradj.first_mention_attestation: No pre-867 CE attestation; desert oasis in Nalut District, northwestern Libya, along the route to Ghadames.

morphemes.translation: steps, degree, or indigenous oasis name

b_daradj.etymology_analysis: Libyan oasis toponym Daraj/Derj (Arabic Daraj), situated on the caravan junction between Nalut and Ghadames; no documented attestation <= 867 CE.

b_tozeur.first_mention_attestation: Roman-era epigraphy and itineraries (Tusuros/Thusuros, 2nd century CE) and 9th-century Arabic geographer al-Ya'qubi (Tuzar).
b_tozeur.etymology_analysis: Arabic Tuzar (French Tozeur) continues the ancient oasis name attested in Latin as Tusuros or Thusuros, of pre-Roman Berber or Afroasiatic origin.

b_taqyus.first_mention_attestation: Roman-era civitas Tigensium / Thiges (2nd century CE) and 9th-century Arabic geographer al-Ya'qubi (Taqyus).

morphemes.translation: Taqyus (ancient oasis of Thiges near Degache)

b_taqyus.etymology_analysis: Medieval Arabic Taqyus (modern Kriz/Degache area in the Djerid) is the direct phonological continuation of Roman Thiges (civitas Tigensium).

b_hamma.first_mention_attestation: 9th-century Arabic geographer al-Ya'qubi (Kitab al-Buldan, c. 891 CE, reflecting earlier Umayyad/Aghlabid-era Castillia cities) as al-Hamma.
b_hamma.etymology_analysis: Arabic al-Hamma ('the hot spring'), referring to the numerous thermal springs of El Hamma du Jerid, exploited since Roman antiquity.

b_nafta.first_mention_attestation: Late Roman/Byzantine episcopal lists (Nepte, 5th–7th centuries CE) and late Umayyad / 9th-century Arabic sources (Nafta).
b_nafta.etymology_analysis: Arabic Nafta (French Nefta) is the direct continuation of ancient Nepte, an oasis settlement and Roman-Byzantine episcopal see in the Djerid.

b_madas.first_mention_attestation: Late Roman Numidian bishopric of Mades (5th century CE).
b_madas.etymology_analysis: Arabic Midas/Madas (French Midès) continues the ancient Roman-Berber settlement and bishopric of Mades in southern Tunisia.

b_souf.first_mention_attestation: 16th-century permanent oasis urbanization (El Oued / Oued Souf) and 17th-century chronicle of Sheikh Mohamed al-Adwani.
b_souf.etymology_analysis: From Berber asif/suf ('river, watercourse'), referring to the underground river system watering the Oued Souf oasis basin in northeastern Algeria; permanent settlement is attested from the 16th century CE.

b_douz.first_mention_attestation: No pre-867 CE attestation; Saharan oasis town in the Nefzaoua region of southern Tunisia.
b_douz.etymology_analysis: Tunisian oasis toponym Duz (French Douz), historically a caravan stop in the Nefzaoua region; no documented attestation <= 867 CE.

b_kairouan.first_mention_attestation: Foundation of al-Qayrawan by Umayyad general Uqba ibn Nafi in 670 CE.

morphemes.translation: the caravan / military camp, resting place

b_kairouan.etymology_analysis: Arabic al-Qayrawan, borrowed via Persian karvan ('caravan, military camp'), founded in 670 CE as the Arab garrison capital of Ifriqiya.

b_jalula.first_mention_attestation: Early Islamic conquest chronicles (battle near Jalula in 654 CE and siege by Mu'awiya ibn Hudayj in 665 CE) on the site of ancient Cululis.
b_jalula.etymology_analysis: Arabic Jallula (modern Aïn Djeloula) is the Arabicized form of Latin Cululis, a Roman-Byzantine fortress west of Kairouan attested during the 7th-century CE Muslim conquest.

b_sabiba.first_mention_attestation: Antonine Itinerary and Roman inscriptions (Sufes, 3rd century CE; Synod of Sufes, 6th century CE).
b_sabiba.etymology_analysis: Arabic Sabiba (modern Sbiba) continues the Roman-Byzantine city name Sufes in Byzacena.

b_raqqada.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 876 CE by the ninth Aghlabid emir Ibrahim II ibn Ahmad as his royal palace-city.

morphemes.translation: resting place / place of sleep (from r-q-d, 'to sleep')

b_raqqada.etymology_analysis: Arabic Raqqada, derived from the root r-q-d ('to sleep, rest'), founded in 876 CE by Aghlabid emir Ibrahim II southwest of Kairouan (post-867 CE).

b_mansuriya.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 946 CE by Fatimid caliph al-Mansur bi-Nasr Allah just south of Kairouan.
b_mansuriya.eponym_details: Named after the third Fatimid caliph al-Mansur bi-Nasr Allah (Abu Tahir Isma'il, r. 946–953 CE), whose regnal title al-Mansur means 'the Victorious'.
b_mansuriya.etymology_analysis: Arabic al-Mansuriya ('the Victorious'), founded in 946 CE by Fatimid caliph al-Mansur bi-Nasr Allah after his victory over Abu Yazid (post-867 CE).

b_al_abbasiya.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 800 CE by the first Aghlabid emir Ibrahim I ibn al-Aghlab southeast of Kairouan.
b_al_abbasiya.eponym_details: Named after the Abbasid Caliphate (al-'Abbasiyya), whose nominal suzerainty Ibrahim I ibn al-Aghlab acknowledged when establishing the palace-city in 800 CE.

morphemes.translation: Abbasid (city), named after the Abbasid dynasty

b_al_abbasiya.etymology_analysis: Arabic al-'Abbasiyya, founded in 800 CE by Ibrahim I ibn al-Aghlab as a royal residence and mint three miles southeast of Kairouan, named in honor of the Abbasid caliphs.

b_tabassa.first_mention_attestation: 1st-century CE Roman military camp of Legio III Augusta at Theveste (c. 75 CE) and Greek Hekatompyle.
b_tabassa.etymology_analysis: Arabic Tibissa/Tabassa (French Tébessa) is the direct phonological continuation of ancient Latin Theveste (Greek Thebeste), an ancient Berber-Punic and Roman city.

b_madila.first_mention_attestation: Notitia Dignitatum / 484 CE Council of Carthage listing the Numidian bishopric of Midila.
b_madila.etymology_analysis: Arabic Madila (Mdila) continues the late antique Numidian town and episcopal see of Midila.

b_maydara.first_mention_attestation: Roman foundation of Ammaedara (Ad Medera) in the 1st century BCE.
b_maydara.etymology_analysis: Arabic Maydara (modern Haïdra) derives directly from Latin Ammaedara / Ad Medera, one of the oldest Roman cities in Africa.

b_maskiyana.first_mention_attestation: Battle of Meskiana (698 CE) between Umayyad commander Hassan ibn al-Nu'man and Berber queen Dihya (al-Kahina).

morphemes.translation: Meskiana (indigenous toponym in the Aures foothills)

b_maskiyana.etymology_analysis: Arabic Maskiyana (French Meskiana) is attested in early Islamic conquest historiography for the 698 CE Battle of Meskiana.

b_al-qasrayn.first_mention_attestation: No pre-867 CE attestation of the Arabic name al-Qasrayn; post-classical Arabic name for the ruins of Roman Cillium.
b_al-qasrayn.etymology_analysis: Arabic al-Qasrayn ('the Two Castles/Palaces', French Kasserine), referring to the monumental Roman ruins (such as the mausolea/fortress) at the site of ancient Cillium.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Roman Flavian foundation inscriptions at Cillium (c. 80 CE) and 544 CE Battle of Cillium
older_name_by_867.notes: Roman colonia and Byzantine stronghold on the exact site of Kasserine.

b_qafsa.first_mention_attestation: Sallust (Bellum Jugurthinum), recording Gaius Marius's capture of Capsa in 106 BCE.
b_qafsa.etymology_analysis: Arabic Qafsa (Gafsa) is the direct phonological continuation of ancient Numidian and Roman Capsa, captured by Marius in 106 BCE and conquered by Arab forces in the 7th century CE.

b_tala.first_mention_attestation: Sallust (Bellum Jugurthinum) and Roman imperial/episcopal records of Thala.
b_tala.etymology_analysis: Arabic Tala (French Thala) continues the ancient Numidian and Roman city name Thala (from Berber tala, 'spring').

b_annaba.first_mention_attestation: Post-1033 CE Hammadid relocation and medieval Arabic name Balad al-'Unnab / 'Annaba (replacing earlier Buna / Hippo Regius).
b_annaba.etymology_analysis: Arabic 'Annaba, shortened from Balad al-'Unnab ('Land/City of Jujubes'), referring to the abundance of jujube trees; it replaced the earlier medieval name Buna (< Hippo Regius) after the 11th century CE.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Late 3rd-century BCE historical records (Hippo Regius, Numidian royal city) and 7th-century CE Arabic Buna
older_name_by_867.notes: Ancient Phoenician-Numidian-Roman port of Hippo Regius (later Hippona/Buna), superseded by the medieval Arabic name 'Annaba.

b_qalama.first_mention_attestation: 2nd-century CE Roman municipium and colonia of Calama (modern Guelma).
b_qalama.etymology_analysis: Arabic Qalama (modern Guelma) is the direct phonological continuation of Roman Calama in Numidia.

b_izan.first_mention_attestation: No pre-867 CE attestation found in the Annaba/Bona region.

morphemes.translation: unattested toponym in the Annaba region

b_izan.etymology_analysis: No historical settlement named Izan is attested in the Annaba region on or before 867 CE.

b_constantine.first_mention_attestation: Rebuilt and renamed Colonia Constantiniana (Constantina) in 313 CE under Emperor Constantine the Great.
b_constantine.eponym_details: Named after Roman Emperor Constantine the Great (Flavius Valerius Constantinus, r. 306–337 CE), who rebuilt the city in 313 CE after its destruction in 311 CE.
b_constantine.etymology_analysis: English Constantine (Arabic Qusantina) derives from Latin Constantina, bestowed in 313 CE in honor of Emperor Constantine the Great upon the ancient Numidian capital Cirta.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Late 3rd-century BCE historical records (capital of Massylii king Syphax)
older_name_by_867.notes: Ancient Berber/Numidian capital on the exact site before being renamed Constantina in 313 CE.

b_qasr-al-ifriqi.first_mention_attestation: Fatimid campaign of Ghazwiyya ibn Yusuf (c. 907–908 CE), which reached Qasr al-Ifriqi en route to Tabrashq.
b_qasr-al-ifriqi.etymology_analysis: Arabic Qasr al-Ifriqi ('Castle of the Ifriqiyan/African'), a medieval fortress in eastern Algeria attested in early 10th-century CE Fatimid conquest accounts (post-867 CE).

b_tijis.first_mention_attestation: Early 4th-century CE ecclesiastical records (Tigisis in Numidia, 304 CE) and Procopius's History of the Vandal War (6th century CE).

morphemes.translation: Tijis (ancient fortified town of Tigisis in Numidia)

b_tijis.etymology_analysis: Arabic Tijis is the direct continuation of ancient Tigisis in Numidia, fortified under Justinian I and attested in medieval Islamic chronicles.

b_tifash.first_mention_attestation: Carthaginian trading post tp'tn (2nd century BCE) and Roman Tipasa in Numidia.

morphemes.translation: Tifash (from Punic tp'tn, 'place of passage / stopover')

b_tifash.etymology_analysis: Arabic Tifash (Tiffesh) continues Latin Tipasa in Numidia, derived from the Punic trading-post name tp'tn ('place of passage' or 'stopover').

b_taburshiq.first_mention_attestation: Roman municipium elevated by Emperor Trajan c. 100 CE (Municipium Ulpium Traianum Augustum Thubursicu).
b_taburshiq.etymology_analysis: Arabic Taburshiq (also Tabrashq; modern Khamissa/Khemissa) is the Arabicized form of ancient Thubursicum Numidarum.

b_labda.first_mention_attestation: Punic foundation lpq / lpqy (late 7th century BCE) and Roman Leptis Magna (Arabic Labda).
b_labda.etymology_analysis: Arabic Labda (Libda al-Kubra) continues Punic lpq/lpqy and Latin Lepcis/Leptis (Magna), a major Phoenician and Roman city in Tripolitania.

b_tawurgha.first_mention_attestation: Ibn Khaldun (late 14th century CE) in Kitab al-Ibar mentions the Tawergha oasis/tribe on the eastern edge of Hawwara territory.

morphemes.translation: green-yellow / verdant (referring to the green oasis)

b_tawurgha.etymology_analysis: From Berber Tawerɣa, meaning 'the green island' or 'verdant place', referring to the fertile palm oasis south of Misrata. While the region was traversed in Roman and early Islamic times, the Berber toponym Tawergha is not attested in written sources prior to the late medieval period (e.g., Ibn Khaldun, 14th century CE).

b_misurata.first_mention_attestation: Al-Bakri (1068 CE) and later medieval Arabic geographers record the Misrata tribe/settlement on the Tripolitanian coast.
b_misurata.eponym_details: Named after the Misrata (Misratah) tribe, a sub-tribe of the Berber Hawwara confederation.

morphemes.translation: ethnonym of the Misrata Berber tribe

b_misurata.etymology_analysis: Named after the Misrata tribe, a branch of the Berber Hawwara confederation (Arabic Miṣrāta, Italianized as Misurata). The classical Phoenician and Roman port at or near the site was known as Thubactis (also Tubartis / Cephalae Promontorium), whereas the tribal name Misrata is only attested in post-867 CE medieval Arabic sources.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Strabo (Geography, c. 20 CE) and Roman itineraries (Tabula Peutingeriana, 4th century CE)
older_name_by_867.notes: Ancient Phoenician/Roman trading station of Thubactis (Strabo's Cephalae Promontorium) preceded the medieval tribal name Misrata.

b_syrte.first_mention_attestation: Ibn Abd al-Hakam (d. 871 CE, Futuh Misr wa'l-Maghrib) records the early Muslim conquest of Surt (642–643 CE), deriving from Classical Syrtis (Herodotus, 5th century BCE).

morphemes.translation: sandbank, shoal, or gulf (Gulf of Sidra)

b_syrte.etymology_analysis: From Ancient Greek Syrtis (Latin Syrtis, Arabic Surt, French/Italian Syrte/Sirte), originally denoting the treacherous sandbanks and gulf of the Greater Syrtis (Herodotus, 5th century BCE). The medieval Berber-Arab town of Surt is attested in Ibn Abd al-Hakam's account of the 642–643 CE Arab conquest.

b_al_aghaila.first_mention_attestation: Modern Arabic toponym al-Uqayla (El Agheila), documented prominently in the early 20th century CE during Italian colonial rule.

morphemes.translation: diminutive of ʿaqla (small stronghold, bend, or hobble)

b_al_aghaila.etymology_analysis: Arabic al-ʿUqayla (transliterated Al Aghaila / El Agheila), a diminutive form from the root ʿ-q-l ('bend, enclosure, or stronghold'). The modern Arabic name is post-867 CE, occupying the site of ancient Greek Automala (4th century BCE) and Roman Anabucis (4th century CE).

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Diodorus Siculus (recording Ophellas's 309–308 BCE camp at Automala) and Tabula Peutingeriana (4th century CE, Anabucis)
older_name_by_867.notes: El Agheila sits on the site of the Greek settlement Automala and the Roman fortified town of Anabucis.

b_ajadabiya.first_mention_attestation: Ibn Abd al-Hakam (d. 871 CE, Futuh Misr wa'l-Maghrib) records Ajdabiya during the 7th-century CE Muslim conquest of Cyrenaica.

morphemes.translation: medieval oasis town name (of uncertain pre-Islamic/Berber origin)

b_ajadabiya.etymology_analysis: Arabic Ajdābiyā (transliterated Ajadabiya / Ajdabiya), attested in early Islamic historiography (Ibn Abd al-Hakam, d. 871 CE) as a key staging post in Cyrenaica/Syrtica. It stands on or near the site of the Roman military station Corniclanum (Tabula Peutingeriana, 4th century CE).

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Tabula Peutingeriana (4th century CE Roman military station Corniclanum)
older_name_by_867.notes: Built on or near the site of the Roman military station Corniclanum.

b_waddan.first_mention_attestation: Ibn Abd al-Hakam (d. 871 CE, Futuh Misr wa'l-Maghrib) records the capture of Waddan by Busr ibn Abi Artat in 642 CE and its reconquest by Uqba ibn Nafi in 666–667 CE.

morphemes.translation: oasis town in the Jufra depression (possibly linked to Berber waddan 'Barbary sheep' or local toponym)

b_waddan.etymology_analysis: Arabic Waddān (transliterated Waddan), the oldest oasis town in the al-Jufra region of central Libya. Attested in early Islamic conquest narratives for 642 CE and 666–667 CE (Ibn Abd al-Hakam, d. 871 CE).

b_tajrift.first_mention_attestation: Documented in 1928 CE as Bir Tagrift, site of the Battle of Bir Tagrift during the Italian pacification of Libya.
b_tajrift.etymology_analysis: From Berber Tagrift (also Tajrift / Bir Tagrift), a desert depression in the Sirtica region of Libya. No pre-867 CE historical attestation exists; the name is known from the 1928 CE Battle of Bir Tagrift.

b_tinnai.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in historical sources; no pre-867 CE or medieval record found for a settlement named Tinnai near Waddan.
b_tinnai.etymology_analysis: Tinnai is unattested in classical, medieval Arabic, or modern Libyan historical geography for the Waddan/Jufra region; its origin and date of attestation are unknown.

b_jerba.first_mention_attestation: Aurelius Victor (4th century CE, De Caesaribus) states that Trebonianus Gallus and Volusianus were proclaimed emperors in 251 CE on the island of Meninx, 'now called Girba'; also appears as Girba on the Tabula Peutingeriana (4th–5th century CE).
b_jerba.etymology_analysis: Modern Jerba (French Djerba, Arabic Jirba) derives directly from Latin Girba, attested by the 3rd–4th century CE (Aurelius Victor, 4th century CE, referring to 251 CE) as the newer name of the island previously called Meninx.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Pliny the Elder, Naturalis Historia 5.41 (77 CE) and Aurelius Victor, De Caesaribus 31 ('the island of Meninx, now called Girba')
older_name_by_867.notes: Known in classical antiquity as Meninx prior to the Late Roman/medieval form Girba / Jerba.

b_jarjis.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Gergis in the Stadiasmus Maris Magni (c. 1st–3rd century CE) and Roman-era sources.

morphemes.translation: coastal port name (adapted in Arabic as Jarjīs / Zarzis)

b_jarjis.etymology_analysis: Arabic Jarjīs (French Zarzis) is the direct phonetic continuation of ancient Punic/Roman Gergis, attested in classical periplus literature (Stadiasmus Maris Magni) and Roman ecclesiastical records.

b_bughrara.first_mention_attestation: Modern Tunisian village name Boughrara (Sidi Salem Boughrara), documented in 19th-century CE geographical and archaeological surveys (Victor Guérin, 1860 CE).
b_bughrara.etymology_analysis: Tunisian Arabic Būġrāra (French Boughrara), a post-867 CE settlement name adjacent to the ancient Punic and Roman port city of Gigthis (attested from the 1st century CE).

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Pliny the Elder (Naturalis Historia, 77 CE), Ptolemy, and Tabula Peutingeriana
older_name_by_867.notes: Modern Boughrara lies directly adjacent to the ruins of ancient Punic-Roman Gigthis.

b_zuwara.first_mention_attestation: Abdallah al-Tijani (Rihla, 1306–1309 CE) provides the earliest mention of Zuwara as Zwara al-soughra and Zwara al-koubra.
b_zuwara.etymology_analysis: Arabic Zuwāra (Berber Azwār), first attested in 1306–1309 CE by the Tunisian traveler Abdallah al-Tijani, and later in the 1375 CE Catalan Atlas as Punta dar Zoyara.

b_tiri.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in historical sources; no pre-867 CE or medieval record found for a settlement named Tiri in Jafara/Tripolitania.
b_tiri.etymology_analysis: Tiri is unattested in classical, medieval Arabic, or modern historical sources for the Jafara plain or Tripolitania; its etymology and earliest attestation are unknown.

b_djado_jafara.first_mention_attestation: Al-Bakri (Kitab al-Masalik wa'l-Mamalik, 1068 CE) mentions Jadu (Djado) and its Jewish community in the Nafusa Mountains.

morphemes.translation: town name in the Nafusa Mountains

b_djado_jafara.etymology_analysis: Jādū (French Djado), a Berber trade town in the Nafusa Mountains of Tripolitania. Its earliest documented attestation is in al-Bakri's 11th-century CE geographical work (1068 CE).

b_nalut.first_mention_attestation: Oldest dated monument (Alal'a Mosque) rebuilt in 1312 CE; earliest mentions of Nalut appear in post-867 CE medieval Ibadi/Maghrebi chronicles.
b_nalut.eponym_details: Possibly linked to Tala, a pre-Islamic Berber goddess of springs.

morphemes.translation: town name (possibly from Tala, Berber deity of springs)

b_nalut.etymology_analysis: Berber Nālūt (alternatively Lalūt), possibly derived from Tala, a pagan Berber goddess of springs. Although an important caravan town in the Nafusa Mountains, no written attestation of the name exists on or before 867 CE.

b_fursata.first_mention_attestation: Attested in 10th-century CE Ibadi sources (cited in al-Shammakhi's Kitab al-Siyar) as Fursata / Fasatu.

morphemes.translation: from African Romance *Fossato < Latin fossatum ('ditch, fortified camp')

b_fursata.etymology_analysis: Fursāṭā (Berber Fassâṭo, Arabic Fursata/Fasatu) derives from African Romance *Fossato, from Latin fossatum ('ditch, fortification') along the Roman-Byzantine limes. The toponym is first attested in 10th-century CE Ibadi historical accounts.

b_libtripoli.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Tripolis / Regio Tripolitana in 4th-century CE Roman sources and as Tarabulus in Ibn Abd al-Hakam's account of the 643 CE Arab conquest.

morphemes.translation: city (referring to Oea, Sabratha, and Leptis Magna)

b_libtripoli.etymology_analysis: From Ancient Greek Tripolis ('Three Cities', Latin Tripolitana, Arabic Ṭarābulus), originally referring to the federation of Oea, Sabratha, and Leptis Magna, and by the 4th–7th centuries CE applied specifically to Oea (modern Tripoli).

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Pliny the Elder, Naturalis Historia 5.27 (77 CE); Phoenician/Punic city of Oea
older_name_by_867.notes: Originally Phoenician/Roman Oea, one of the three cities of Regio Tripolitana, before the regional name Tripolis attached specifically to Oea in Late Antiquity.

b_sabratha.first_mention_attestation: Established c. 500 BCE as Phoenician Tsabratan (Punic ṣbrtn), later Greek Sabrata/Abrotonon and Latin Sabratha (Pliny, Ptolemy).

morphemes.translation: pre-Phoenician Berber toponym adapted into Punic as Tsabratan

b_sabratha.etymology_analysis: From Phoenician-Punic Tsabratan (ṣbrtn / ṣbrtʿn, c. 500 BCE), itself adapting a pre-existing Berber name, Hellenized as Sabrata and Latinized as Sabratha.

b_tamazda.first_mention_attestation: Mentioned in Ahmad ibn Sa'id al-Shammakhi's Kitab al-Siyar (c. 1500 CE, d. 1522 CE); no written attestation of the name Tamazda is documented <= 867 CE.

morphemes.translation: settlement name in the Nafusa Mountains

b_tamazda.etymology_analysis: Berber settlement name Tamazda (Temezda) in the Nafusa Mountains. Although its Kanisa Mosque was converted from an earlier Byzantine church in the 8th–9th centuries CE, the toponym itself is first attested in al-Shammakhi's Kitab al-Siyar (early 16th century CE).

b_mahdiya.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 916 CE (officially inaugurated in 921 CE) by the first Fatimid Caliph, Ubayd Allah al-Mahdi Billah.
b_mahdiya.eponym_details: Named after Ubayd Allah al-Mahdi Billah (r. 909–934 CE), founder of the Fatimid Caliphate.

morphemes.translation: city of al-Mahdi (from Ubayd Allah al-Mahdi)

b_mahdiya.etymology_analysis: Arabic al-Mahdiyya (French Mahdia), founded in 916 CE and named after the Fatimid Caliph Ubayd Allah al-Mahdi Billah. It was built on the peninsula of the ancient Phoenician and Roman port of Aphrodisium.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Claudius Ptolemy (Geography, 2nd century CE) and Roman itineraries
older_name_by_867.notes: The old peninsula of Mahdia corresponds to the ancient Phoenician and Roman port city of Aphrodisium.

b_monastir.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 796 CE with the construction of the Ribat of Monastir by Abbasid governor Harthama ibn A'yan.

morphemes.translation: from Greek monastḗrion / Latin monasterium ('monastery, hermit's cell')

b_monastir.etymology_analysis: Arabic al-Munastīr (Monastir), borrowed from Byzantine Greek monastḗrion (Latin monasterium, 'monastery'), referring to a pre-Islamic Christian monastic complex on the site before Harthama ibn A'yan built the Ribat of Monastir in 796 CE.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Bellum Africum (46 BCE, Julius Caesar's African campaign)
older_name_by_867.notes: Adjacent to ancient Punic/Roman Ruspina prior to the Abbasid foundation of the Ribat of Monastir in 796 CE.

b_susa.first_mention_attestation: Aghlabid port of Susa (Sousse), where Ziyadat Allah I renovated the Ribat in 821 CE (206 AH), followed by the kasbah (844 CE) and city walls (859 CE).

morphemes.translation: early Islamic port town established near ancient Hadrumetum

b_susa.etymology_analysis: Arabic Sūsa (French Sousse), established under the Aghlabids in the early 9th century CE near the ruins of ancient Hadrumetum (later Justinianopolis), with the Ribat rebuilt in 821 CE.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Ancient Punic/Roman Hadrumetum (6th–5th century BCE) and Byzantine Justinianopolis (6th century CE)
older_name_by_867.notes: Aghlabid Susa (Sousse) overlies the ancient Punic/Roman port of Hadrumetum, renamed Justinianopolis under Justinian I.

b_baja_medjerda.first_mention_attestation: Sallust (Bellum Jugurthinum, c. 40 BCE) records Vaga during the Jugurthine War (109–108 BCE), later Arabicized as Baja.
b_baja_medjerda.etymology_analysis: Arabic Bāja (French Béja) is the direct phonetic evolution of ancient Waga / Latin Vaga (Greek Vacca in Plutarch), attested in Sallust's account of the Jugurthine War (109–108 BCE).

b_siqqabanariya.first_mention_attestation: Polybius (Histories, 1.66) records Sicca during the Mercenary War (c. 241 BCE), later Roman Sicca Veneria, Arabicized as Siqqabanariya / Shaqbanariya.
b_siqqabanariya.eponym_details: Veneria refers to the Roman goddess Venus (equated with Punic Astarte), whose temple stood in the city.

morphemes.translation: of Venus (adapted in Arabic as Siqqabanāriya / Shaqbanāriya)

b_siqqabanariya.etymology_analysis: Arabic Siqqabanāriya (Shaqbanāriya) is the direct Arabization of Latin Sicca Veneria (originally Punic-Numidian Sicca, attested by Polybius for c. 241 BCE), which was later replaced by the modern name El Kef in the 16th century CE.

b_al_aribus.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Lares / Laribus in Roman itineraries (4th century CE) and as Laribouzoudoúon in Procopius (6th century CE), passing into Arabic as Laribus / al-Aribus.
b_al_aribus.etymology_analysis: Arabic al-ʿAribus / al-Urbus (modern Henchir Lorbeus) derives directly from Latin Laribus (locative/ablative of Lares), attested in 4th-century CE Roman itineraries and 6th-century CE Byzantine sources (Procopius).

b_banzart.first_mention_attestation: Polybius (Histories, 2nd century BCE) mentions Hippo Diarrhytus (later Hippo Zarytus), from which Arabic Binzart (Banzart/Bizerte) phonetically derives.

morphemes.translation: divided by water (phonetically contracted to Arabic Binzart)

b_banzart.etymology_analysis: Arabic Binzart (Banzart, French Bizerte) is a direct phonetic contraction of Late Latin Hippo Zarytus (from Greek Hippōn diárrhytos, 'Hippo Divided-by-the-Water', attested in Polybius, 2nd century BCE, itself from Punic ʿpwn 'harbor').

b_tabarqa.first_mention_attestation: Pliny the Elder (Naturalis Historia, 77 CE) and Juvenal (Satire 10, early 2nd century CE) attest Thabraca, continuing Punic tbrkʿn.

morphemes.translation: ancient coastal town name (traditionally linked to 'place of shade/mulberries')

b_tabarqa.etymology_analysis: Arabic Ṭabarqa (French Tabarka) is the direct continuation of Punic tbrkʿn, Greek Thaúbraka, and Latin Thabraca, attested by Pliny the Elder (77 CE) and Juvenal.

b_mansa'l-kharaz.first_mention_attestation: Ibn Hawqal (Kitab Surat al-Ard, c. 977 CE) provides the earliest extant mention of Marsa al-Kharaz as a coral-trading port.

morphemes.translation: harbor, port (corrupted in repo key as 'Mansa')

b_mansa'l-kharaz.etymology_analysis: Arabic Marsā al-Kharaz ('Harbor of the Beads/Coral', modern El Kala, Algeria), first attested in the 10th century CE by Ibn Hawqal (c. 977 CE) and later al-Bakri (1068 CE). The site corresponds to the ancient Roman road station Tuniza on the Tabula Peutingeriana.

older_name_by_867.notes: El Kala / Marsa al-Kharaz is identified with the Roman station of Tuniza, 24 miles west of Thabraca.

b_tunis.first_mention_attestation: Diodorus Siculus (World History, 14.77) records Tunes during the 396–395 BCE Libyan revolt against Carthage, and Polybius (1.30, 14.10) describes it in the Punic Wars.

morphemes.translation: ancient Numidian toponym (beginning with Berber feminine prefix t-)

b_tunis.etymology_analysis: Arabic Tūnis continues Greek Týnēs / Latin Tunes, a pre-Roman Numidian-Berber toponym attested by Diodorus Siculus for 396–395 BCE and Polybius in the 3rd–2nd centuries BCE.

b_zaghwan.first_mention_attestation: Al-Bakri (Kitab al-Masalik wa'l-Mamalik, 1068 CE) provides the earliest extant medieval Arabic attestation of Zaghwan.

morphemes.translation: medieval town name on the site of Roman Ziqua

b_zaghwan.etymology_analysis: Arabic Zaghwān (French Zaghouan), first attested in medieval Arabic geography by al-Bakri (1068 CE). The town occupies the site of the ancient Roman municipium of Ziqua (Zica / Zigus), source of the 2nd-century CE Carthage aqueduct.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Roman epigraphy and ecclesiastical lists (2nd–5th centuries CE)
older_name_by_867.notes: Zaghouan is built directly on the site of the ancient Roman city of Ziqua (also spelled Zica / Zigus).

b_qartajana.first_mention_attestation: Founded traditionally in 814 BCE by Phoenicians from Tyre as Qart-Hadasht (recorded by Timaeus of Tauromenium, c. 300 BCE), Latin Carthago, Arabicized as Qartajana.

morphemes.translation: new (adapted via Latin Carthago into Arabic Qarṭājanna)

b_qartajana.etymology_analysis: Arabic Qarṭājanna is the direct Arabization of Latin Carthago, from Phoenician-Punic Qart-Ḥadašt ('New City'), traditionally founded in 814 BCE.

b_nabeul.first_mention_attestation: Founded in the 5th century BCE by Greeks of Cyrene as Neapolis (attested in Thucydides and Classical Greek/Roman sources), Arabicized as Nabil (Nabeul).
b_nabeul.etymology_analysis: Arabic Nābil (French Nabeul) is the direct Arabization of Ancient Greek Neápolis ('New City'), founded in the 5th century BCE by Greek colonists from Cyrene.

b_silyana.first_mention_attestation: Modern farming town of Siliana was founded in 1905 CE (municipality created in 1945 CE).

morphemes.translation: modern town name (named after Oued Siliana)

b_silyana.etymology_analysis: Tunisian Arabic Silyāna (Siliana), a modern agricultural town founded in 1905 CE on the Oued Siliana, about 10 km from ancient Zama (site of the 202 BCE Battle of Zama).

b_gabes.first_mention_attestation: Pliny the Elder (Naturalis Historia, 77 CE) and Roman itineraries attest Tacapae, from which Arabic Qabis (Gabes) directly evolved.

morphemes.translation: ancient oasis town name (Arabicized as Qābis / Gabès after dropping Berber ta-)

b_gabes.etymology_analysis: Arabic Qābis (Tunisian Gābis, French Gabès) derives from ancient Berber-Punic Takapes / Latin Tacapae (attested by Pliny the Elder, 77 CE), via loss of the Berber prefix ta- and Arabic phonetic adaptation of /p/ to /b/.

b_al_hamma.first_mention_attestation: Al-Bakri (Kitab al-Masalik wa'l-Mamalik, 1068 CE) provides the earliest medieval Arabic attestation of the thermal springs of al-Hamma near Gabes.

morphemes.translation: hot spring / thermal bath (from al-māʾ al-ḥāmm)

b_al_hamma.etymology_analysis: Arabic al-Ḥāmma ('the hot spring/bath'), referring to the natural artesian thermal springs west of Gabes. First attested in Arabic by al-Bakri (1068 CE), the site was known in Roman antiquity as Aquae Tacapitanae.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Antonine Itinerary (3rd century CE) and Tabula Peutingeriana (4th century CE)
older_name_by_867.notes: Roman thermal spa town of Aquae Tacapitanae ('Waters of Tacapae') preceded the Arabic name al-Hamma.

b_amatlus.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in pre-867 CE or medieval historical sources; appears in modern game geography for the Inchiri/Adrar region of Mauritania.

morphemes.translation: unattested toponym (possibly related to Erg Amatlich)

b_amatlus.etymology_analysis: Unattested toponym in historical Arabic and Berber sources; likely a modern or game-adapted rendering of a local Mauritanian/Zenaga Berber name (compare Erg Amatlich in Adrar/Inchiri).

b_akjoujt.first_mention_attestation: Prehistoric copper metallurgy at nearby Guelb Moghrein dates to c. 1000 BCE, but the Berber toponym Akjoujt ('wells') is unattested in pre-867 CE or medieval written sources.
b_akjoujt.etymology_analysis: From Berber (Zenaga) meaning 'wells'. Although copper mining at nearby Guelb Moghrein dates back to c. 1000 BCE, the settlement name Akjoujt is not attested in pre-867 CE or medieval written sources.

b_ijil.first_mention_attestation: Gomes Eanes de Zurara, Chronique de Guinée (1453 CE), and Alvise Cadamosto (1455 CE) on the trans-Saharan salt trade.

morphemes.translation: salt pan / mountain (compare Kediet ej Jill)

b_ijil.etymology_analysis: Berber (Zenaga) toponym referring to the Sebkha of Ijil salt pan in northern Mauritania, first documented in 15th-century CE Portuguese accounts of the trans-Saharan salt trade (Zurara 1453 CE, Cadamosto 1455 CE).

b_azukki.first_mention_attestation: Al-Bakri, Kitab al-Masalik wa-l-Mamalik (1068 CE), recording the Almoravid fortress at Azuggi/Azukki.
b_azukki.etymology_analysis: Sanhaja Berber toponym (Arabicized as Azuki/Azuggi) for the oasis and Almoravid fortress near Atar in the Adrar Plateau; although 7th-century CE rock carvings exist at the site, the name is first attested by al-Bakri in 1068 CE.

b_wadan.first_mention_attestation: Founded c. 1147 CE during the Almoravid period; later documented in 15th-century CE Portuguese accounts (1487 CE).
b_wadan.etymology_analysis: From Arabic Wādān ('Two Wadis'), dual form of wādī ('valley/seasonal river'), referring to the oasis town founded c. 1147 CE on the southern edge of the Adrar Plateau.

b_tingi.first_mention_attestation: Founded in the 12th century CE by the Tajakant (Tadjakant) tribe between Chinguetti and Ouadane in the Mauritanian Adrar.
b_tingi.etymology_analysis: Sanhaja Berber toponym (Tinigui) for a vanished medieval caravan town founded in the 12th century CE by the Tajakant between Chinguetti and Ouadane.

b_shinqiti.first_mention_attestation: Traditional founding dated to 777 CE as a caravan oasis in the Mauritanian Adrar.
b_shinqiti.etymology_analysis: From Azer (a Soninke-Berber contact dialect) meaning 'spring of horses' (Arabicized as Shinqīṭ / Shinqīṭī); traditionally founded in 777 CE.

b_agharaf_road.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in pre-867 CE historical sources; modern/game desert corridor designation in the Mauritanian Adrar.
b_agharaf_road.etymology_analysis: Modern/game desert-corridor name combining a local Berber/Hassaniya toponym (Agharaf) with English 'Road'; unattested as a historical title <= 867 CE.

b_wadi_daoura.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in pre-867 CE historical sources; documented as a Saharan wadi in modern geographical literature.
b_wadi_daoura.etymology_analysis: Hydronym combining Arabic wādī ('intermittent river/valley') with Daoura; unattested in pre-867 CE historical sources.

b_iguidi_east.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in pre-867 CE historical sources; modern/game directional subdivision of the Erg Iguidi sand sea.
b_iguidi_east.etymology_analysis: Modern/game directional subdivision ('East') of the Erg Iguidi sand sea in the southwestern Sahara; unattested <= 867 CE.

b_saoura.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in pre-867 CE historical sources; documented as a Saharan valley and region in later Arabic and modern geography.
b_saoura.etymology_analysis: Regional choronym and hydronym from Oued Saoura (Arabic al-Sāwira, Berber Asawira) in southwestern Algeria; unattested in pre-867 CE sources.

b_taghaza_road.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in pre-867 CE historical sources; modern/game desert corridor named after the medieval salt-mining center of Taghaza.
b_taghaza_road.etymology_analysis: Modern/game caravan-route designation combining the Berber toponym Taghaza (first attested in the 14th century CE) with English 'Road'.

b_taghaza.first_mention_attestation: Ibn Battuta, Rihla (1352 CE), describing the salt-mining village of Taghaza on the trans-Saharan caravan route.
b_taghaza.etymology_analysis: Berber toponym (Arabicized as Taghāza / Teghāza) for the Saharan salt-mining oasis in northern Mali, first documented by Ibn Battuta in 1352 CE.

b_taoudeni.first_mention_attestation: Established c. 1586 CE as the replacement salt-mining center after the Saadian occupation of Taghaza.
b_taoudeni.etymology_analysis: Berber (Tuareg Tawdenni, Arabic Tawdannī) name for the salt-pan oasis in northern Mali that replaced Taghaza as the primary Saharan salt mine after 1586 CE.

b_tamentit.first_mention_attestation: Local Touati chronicle by al-Amuri (recording events of 1435 CE in Tamentit, cited by A. G. P. Martin); ksar tradition dates to the 12th century CE.
b_tamentit.etymology_analysis: From Zenata Berber Tam-n-tit ('eyebrow/perfection of the spring' or 'end of the spring', from tit 'spring/eye'); unattested in pre-867 CE sources, with the ksar emerging in the 12th century CE and first documented in 1435 CE.

b_reggane.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in pre-867 CE sources; an oasis at the southern end of Touat formalized administratively in 1902 CE.
b_reggane.etymology_analysis: From Berber Argan (Arabicized as Raqqān / Reggane), an oasis at the southern end of the Touat corridor; unattested in pre-867 CE written sources.

b_hamadat_tinghert.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in pre-867 CE historical sources; modern geographical name for the Tinrhert rocky plateau in the Algerian Sahara.
b_hamadat_tinghert.etymology_analysis: Topographic name combining Arabic ḥamāda ('rocky desert plateau') with the Berber (Tuareg) name Tinghert/Tinrhert; unattested <= 867 CE.

b_tidikelt.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in pre-867 CE historical sources; oasis group south of Touat documented in post-medieval Saharan and modern geographical sources.

morphemes.translation: palm of the hand (metaphor for a flat plain/basin)

b_tidikelt.etymology_analysis: From Zenata Berber Tidikelt ('palm of the hand', referring to the flat Saharan basin); unattested in pre-867 CE written sources.

b_adrar_timmi.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in pre-867 CE historical sources; Adrar (historically Timmi) developed as a Touat oasis ksar in the post-867 CE Islamic period.
b_adrar_timmi.etymology_analysis: Combines Berber Adrar ('mountain', or shortened from plural Adghaghen) with Timmi, the name of the local Berber group that established the ksar; unattested <= 867 CE.

b_bouda.first_mention_attestation: Ibn Battuta, Rihla (1353 CE), describing Būda as 'one of the biggest villages of the Tuwāt'.
b_bouda.etymology_analysis: Zenata Berber toponym (Arabicized as Būda) for one of the oldest oasis settlements in northern Touat, first attested in writing by Ibn Battuta in 1353 CE.

b_tabalbala.first_mention_attestation: Attested from the 13th century CE (c. 1200–1300 CE) as a trans-Saharan caravan stop between Sijilmasa and Timbuktu.
b_tabalbala.etymology_analysis: Berber toponym (Tabelbalt, Arabicized as Tabalbāla) for the isolated oasis founded around 1200 CE (13th century CE) along the Sijilmasa–Timbuktu caravan route.

b_tindouf.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1852 CE by the Tajakant tribe near a Saharan oasis (name possibly linked to al-Bakri's 11th-century Tendefes wells).
b_tindouf.etymology_analysis: Berber toponym (variously derived from tidaf 'sentinel', tin-oudhef 'place of allocation', or al-Bakri's Tendefes 'temporary wells'); the town itself was founded in 1852 CE by the Tajakant.

b_tindouf_road.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in pre-867 CE historical sources; modern/game desert corridor named after Tindouf (founded 1852 CE).
b_tindouf_road.etymology_analysis: Modern/game desert-corridor designation combining the Berber toponym Tindouf (town founded 1852 CE) with English 'Road'; unattested <= 867 CE.

b_iguidi_west.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in pre-867 CE historical sources; modern/game directional subdivision of the Erg Iguidi sand sea.
b_iguidi_west.etymology_analysis: Modern/game directional subdivision ('West') of the Erg Iguidi sand sea in the southwestern Sahara; unattested <= 867 CE.

b_bir_um-ghrein.first_mention_attestation: 20th-century settlement established in the 1930s CE as French Fort-Trinquet and renamed Bir Moghrein in 1969 CE.
b_bir_um-ghrein.etymology_analysis: From Hassaniya Arabic Biʾr Umm Ghrīn ('Well of Moghrein'); the modern town originated as French colonial Fort-Trinquet in the 1930s CE and was renamed Bir Moghrein in 1969 CE.

b_tiris.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in pre-867 CE written sources; a pre-Arabic Berber regional name documented in modern Mauritanian and Saharan scholarship.
b_tiris.etymology_analysis: Pre-Arabic Berber choronym for the arid plains of northern Mauritania and southern Western Sahara; unattested in written sources <= 867 CE.

b_tiris-south.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in pre-867 CE historical sources; modern/game directional subdivision of the Tiris region.
b_tiris-south.etymology_analysis: Modern/game directional subdivision ('South') of the Berber choronym Tiris; unattested <= 867 CE.

b_zammour.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in pre-867 CE written sources; a pre-Arabic Berber regional toponym in Western Sahara and northern Mauritania.
b_zammour.etymology_analysis: From Berber azemmur ('wild olive tree'), a pre-Arabic regional choronym in Western Sahara and northern Mauritania; unattested in written sources <= 867 CE.

b_sequiet_el-hamra.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in pre-867 CE written sources; Arabic hydronym and region name emerging after Arabization from the 11th–14th centuries CE.
b_sequiet_el-hamra.etymology_analysis: From Arabic al-Sāqiya al-Ḥamrāʾ ('the Red Canal/Channel'), referring to the reddish-soiled intermittent wadi in northern Western Sahara; post-dates the 867 CE baseline.

b_agadez.first_mention_attestation: Leo Africanus, Descrittione dell'Africa (1526 CE); founded in the early 15th century CE (c. 1405–1449 CE) as capital of the Sultanate of Aïr.
b_agadez.etymology_analysis: From Tamajeq (Tuareg Berber) Agadaz (from the root gdz, 'to visit'), reflecting its role as a seasonal caravan encampment and trading crossroads founded in the early 15th century CE.

b_air.first_mention_attestation: Leo Africanus, Descrittione dell'Africa (1526 CE), as 'Air' (also 'Asben').
b_air.etymology_analysis: From Tamajeq (Tuareg Berber) Ayǝr, the indigenous name of the Aïr Mountains massif in northern Niger; first attested in external written sources by Leo Africanus in 1526 CE.

b_fachi_route.first_mention_attestation: Unattested as a historical settlement name; modern English game-design label for the caravan route between Aïr and Fachi.
b_fachi_route.etymology_analysis: Modern English compound combining the oasis name Fachi (Tuareg/Hausa name for the oasis called Agram in Kanuri/Toubou) with 'Route' to represent the trans-Ténéré Azalay salt caravan trail.

b_takkeda.etymology_analysis: Berber/Tamajeq toponym (variously linked to Tegidda, 'water-source/salt-spring'); although copperworking at Azelik wan Birni dates to the 1st millennium BCE, the name Takedda is first attested in writing by Ibn Battuta in 1353 CE.

b_marandet.first_mention_attestation: Al-Ya'qubi, Ta'rikh (872 CE), as 'Maranda'; archaeologically active 6th–10th centuries CE.
b_marandet.etymology_analysis: Identified with medieval Maranda, a copper-working and trans-Saharan trade center attested in Arabic geography starting with al-Ya'qubi in 872 CE (five years after the 867 CE baseline).

b_air_route.first_mention_attestation: Unattested as a historical settlement name; modern English game-design label for the caravan route through Aïr.
b_air_route.etymology_analysis: Modern English compound combining the regional oronym Aïr (Tamajeq Ayǝr) with 'Route' to represent a trans-Saharan caravan corridor.

b_germa.first_mention_attestation: Pliny the Elder, Naturalis Historia (c. 77 CE), as 'Garama caput Garamantum'; later Ptolemy (c. 150 CE).
b_germa.etymology_analysis: Ancient Garamantian capital Garama (attested in Pliny c. 77 CE and Ptolemy c. 150 CE), surviving in Arabic as Jarma / Germa.

b_sabha.first_mention_attestation: Pliny the Elder, Naturalis Historia (c. 77 CE), as 'Sabae' in Phazania; modern Arabic form Sabha attested in later periods.
b_sabha.etymology_analysis: Ancient Fezzan oasis settlement attested in Roman-era sources (Pliny, c. 77 CE) as Sabae, continuing in Arabic as Sabhā (Sebha).

b_tamzawa.first_mention_attestation: No pre-867 CE or medieval written attestation found; modern oasis village in Wadi ash-Shati, Fezzan.
b_tamzawa.etymology_analysis: Oasis village in the Wadi ash-Shati depression of northern Fezzan, Libya; likely of Berber origin (feminine t- prefix) but unattested in historical sources on or before 867 CE.

b_murzuk.first_mention_attestation: Founded c. 1310 CE under the Kanem Empire (construction of Murzuq Castle); later capital of the Awlad Muhammad dynasty (16th century CE).
b_murzuk.etymology_analysis: Arabic Marzūq ('blessed, endowed with sustenance'); founded around 1310 CE under Kanem influence and developed into the capital of Fezzan in the 16th century CE.

b_tassawa.first_mention_attestation: No pre-867 CE written attestation found; oasis village (Tasawah) in Wadi Ataba, Fezzan, Libya.
b_tassawa.etymology_analysis: Oasis village in Wadi Ataba near Murzuk, Fezzan; locally nicknamed 'Little Garama' in tradition, but the name Tassawa/Tasawah is unattested in historical sources on or before 867 CE.

b_traghan.first_mention_attestation: Founded by the Sayfawa dynasty of Kanem in the 13th century CE (c. 1250 CE) as their Fezzan outpost.
b_traghan.etymology_analysis: From Toubou (Gara'an) Taraghan / Turaghan, meaning 'inhabitants of the small land'; established as a Kanem-Bornu administrative center in Fezzan in the 13th century CE.

b_fezzan_route.first_mention_attestation: Unattested as a historical settlement name; modern English game-design label for the Fezzan caravan corridor.
b_fezzan_route.etymology_analysis: Modern English compound combining the regional choronym Fezzan (from Latin Phazania / Berber Ifezzan) with 'Route' to represent a trans-Saharan caravan corridor.

b_zawila.first_mention_attestation: Abbasid conquest of Zawila in 762/763 CE under Muhammad ibn al-Ash'ath al-Khuza'i (recorded in early Islamic historiography and al-Ya'qubi, 891 CE).
b_zawila.etymology_analysis: Early Islamic caravan city settled in the early 8th century CE (absent when Uqba ibn Nafi passed in 666/667 CE), becoming the Ibadi capital of Fezzan by 762/763 CE.

b_zalha.first_mention_attestation: Al-Umari (14th century CE, c. 1337–1349 CE), describing Zella as the northeastern limit of the Kanem Empire.
b_zalha.etymology_analysis: Oasis of Zella (Arabic Zallah) in northeastern Fezzan / Jufra; first clearly attested in medieval Arabic sources by al-Umari in the 14th century CE.

b_djanet.first_mention_attestation: Founded in the Middle Ages by the Kel Ajjer Tuareg; attested in early modern records from the 17th century CE.
b_djanet.etymology_analysis: Tuareg (Kel Ajjer) oasis settlement in the Tassili n'Ajjer; founded in the medieval period with no written attestation on or before 867 CE.

b_eferi.first_mention_attestation: No pre-867 CE written attestation found; modern village in Djanet commune, Algeria.
b_eferi.etymology_analysis: Tuareg-named locality in the Djanet oasis valley at the southwestern edge of Tassili n'Ajjer; unattested in historical sources on or before 867 CE.

b_ahaggar.first_mention_attestation: Ibn Battuta, Rihla (1353 CE) and Ibn Khaldun (late 14th century CE), as 'Hoggar' / 'Ahaggar'.
b_ahaggar.etymology_analysis: From Tamahaq Ahaggar (Arabicized as Hoggar), derived according to Ibn Khaldun from the Berber tribal name Hawwara; first attested in 14th-century CE Arabic sources.

b_east_ahaggar.first_mention_attestation: Unattested as a historical toponym; modern English directional subdivision of the Ahaggar Mountains.
b_east_ahaggar.etymology_analysis: Modern English directional compound ('East' + Ahaggar) created for map subdivision; the underlying oronym Ahaggar is itself unattested before the 14th century CE.

b_ghat.first_mention_attestation: Early modern Fezzan/Kel Ajjer records (17th century CE); first detailed European description by James Richardson (1845–1846 CE).
b_ghat.etymology_analysis: Tuareg Kel Ajjer oasis stronghold in southwestern Fezzan; while the Wadi Tanezzuft hosted Garamantian settlements nearby, the name Ghat itself is unattested on or before 867 CE.

b_al-fewet.first_mention_attestation: No pre-867 CE written attestation found; Garamantian archaeological site (2nd–1st century BCE) beneath modern Fewet oasis.
b_al-fewet.etymology_analysis: Arabic definite article al- prefixed to the local oasis name Fewet near Ghat; Garamantian occupation is archaeologically dated to the 2nd–1st centuries BCE, but the name Al-Fewet has no pre-867 CE written attestation.

b_al-barkat.first_mention_attestation: No pre-867 CE written attestation found; modern oasis near the Garamantian citadel of Aghram Nadharif (1st century BCE–4th century CE).
b_al-barkat.etymology_analysis: Arabic al-Barakāt ('the blessings') or al-Birkah ('the pool/reservoir'); oasis 10 km south of Ghat with nearby Garamantian ruins, unattested by name on or before 867 CE.

b_ghat_route.first_mention_attestation: Unattested as a historical settlement name; modern English game-design label for the Ghat caravan corridor.
b_ghat_route.etymology_analysis: Modern English compound combining the oasis name Ghat with 'Route' to represent a trans-Saharan caravan corridor.

b_wadi_irawan.first_mention_attestation: No pre-867 CE written attestation found; dry valley (wadi) in southwestern Fezzan, Libya.
b_wadi_irawan.etymology_analysis: Hybrid Arabic-Berber topographic name combining Arabic wādī ('valley, dry watercourse') with the Berber name Irawan; unattested in historical sources on or before 867 CE.

b_erg_ghati.first_mention_attestation: No pre-867 CE written attestation found; sand-dune sea (erg) near Ghat, Libya.
b_erg_ghati.etymology_analysis: Arabic/Saharan topographic term erg ('sand sea') paired with the nisba adjective Ghati ('of Ghat'); unattested in historical sources on or before 867 CE.

b_bilma.first_mention_attestation: Al-Idrisi, Nuzhat al-mushtaq (1154 CE), as a salt-producing town of Kawar (Kawar itself is attested in al-Ya'qubi, 891 CE).
b_bilma.etymology_analysis: Major salt-producing oasis of the Kawar escarpment in northeastern Niger; first explicitly attested in Arabic geography by al-Idrisi in 1154 CE.

b_dibela.first_mention_attestation: No pre-867 CE written attestation found; small oasis depression in northeastern Niger.
b_dibela.etymology_analysis: Small oasis and cuesta depression in the Erg of Bilma (northeastern Niger); unattested in written historical sources on or before 867 CE.

b_kawar_road.first_mention_attestation: Unattested as a historical settlement name; modern English game-design label for the Kawar caravan trail.
b_kawar_road.etymology_analysis: Modern English compound combining the oasis region Kawar (attested from al-Ya'qubi in 891 CE and Ibn Abd al-Hakam d. 871 CE) with 'Road' to represent the Bornu–Fezzan caravan route.

b_fachi.first_mention_attestation: No pre-867 CE written attestation found; isolated oasis in the Ténéré desert, Niger.
b_fachi.etymology_analysis: Tuareg and Hausa name for the isolated Ténéré oasis known to its Kanuri and Toubou inhabitants as Agram; unattested in historical sources on or before 867 CE.

b_dirku.first_mention_attestation: No pre-867 CE written attestation found; oasis town in northern Kawar, Niger.
b_dirku.etymology_analysis: Oasis town in the northern Kaouar escarpment that succeeded earlier medieval centers (Seguedine, Gasabi/al-Qasaba); unattested in written sources on or before 867 CE.

b_gissebi.first_mention_attestation: Ibn Abd al-Hakam, Futuh Misr wa-l-Maghrib (recording Uqba ibn Nafi's 666–667 CE raid on Kawar and 'al-Qasaba', later rendered Gasabi / Gissebi).
b_gissebi.etymology_analysis: Local Kawar adaptation (Gasabi / Gissebi) of Arabic al-Qaṣaba ('the citadel'), attested in Ibn Abd al-Hakam's account (d. 871 CE) of Uqba ibn Nafi's 666/667 CE raid on Kawar.

b_djado.first_mention_attestation: Kanem-Bornu records under Mai Dunama Dabbalemi (r. 1203–1243 CE).

morphemes.translation: Djado oasis (possibly after Jadu in Jabal Nafusa)

b_djado.etymology_analysis: Ruined ksar and oasis on the Djado Plateau (known locally as Brao), possibly named after Jadu in Libya's Jabal Nafusa by Ibadi merchants; attested under Kanem-Bornu rule by the early 13th century CE.

b_tummo.first_mention_attestation: No pre-867 CE written attestation found; desert well, pass, and plateau on the Niger–Libya border.
b_tummo.etymology_analysis: Strategic Saharan watering point and pass between Fezzan and Kawar (documented in modern colonial surveys such as Emilio Scarin, 1933 CE); unattested on or before 867 CE.

b_sakadame.first_mention_attestation: Al-Ya'qubi, Kitab al-Buldan (891 CE) and 9th-century Arabic geographers, as Seguedine / Seggedim.
b_sakadame.etymology_analysis: Tuareg/Berber name Sǝggǝdǝm (modern Séguédine / Seggedine) for the northernmost major oasis of the Kawar valley; attested in late 9th-century CE Arabic sources (post-867 CE).

b_djado_route.first_mention_attestation: Unattested as a historical settlement name; modern English game-design label for the Djado caravan trail.
b_djado_route.etymology_analysis: Modern English compound combining the oasis name Djado with 'Route' to represent a trans-Saharan caravan corridor.

b_tadmekka.first_mention_attestation: Ibn Hawqal, Kitab Surat al-Ard (c. 988 CE), as 'Tadmakka'; later detailed by al-Bakri (1068 CE).
b_tadmekka.etymology_analysis: Berber-Arabic compound interpreted by al-Bakri (1068 CE) as 'resembling Mecca' due to its religious and commercial prominence; excavated at Essouk (9th–15th centuries CE), with earliest written attestation by Ibn Hawqal (c. 988 CE).

b_kidal.first_mention_attestation: No pre-867 CE written attestation found; modern town in northeastern Mali.
b_kidal.etymology_analysis: Tuareg settlement in the Adrar des Ifoghas (northeastern Mali); unattested in historical sources on or before 867 CE.

b_tessalit.first_mention_attestation: No pre-867 CE written attestation found; oasis village in Kidal Region, Mali.
b_tessalit.etymology_analysis: Tamasheq toponym (feminine t-...-t circumfix) for a Saharan oasis in northern Mali; unattested in historical sources on or before 867 CE.

b_adrar_iforas.first_mention_attestation: No pre-867 CE written attestation found; massif named after the Ifoghas Tuareg.
b_adrar_iforas.etymology_analysis: From Tamasheq Adrar n Ifoghas ('Mountain of the Ifoghas'); unattested in historical sources on or before 867 CE.

b_tadmekka_route.first_mention_attestation: Unattested as a historical settlement name; modern English game-design label for the Tadmekka caravan trail.
b_tadmekka_route.etymology_analysis: Modern English compound combining the medieval entrepôt name Tadmekka with 'Route' to represent a trans-Saharan caravan corridor.

b_ain_galakka.first_mention_attestation: No pre-867 CE written attestation found; oasis in Borkou, Chad, prominent as a Sanusi zawiya in the early 20th century CE.
b_ain_galakka.etymology_analysis: Hybrid Arabic-Toubou toponym combining Arabic ʿayn ('spring') with local Galakka; unattested in historical sources on or before 867 CE.

b_faya.first_mention_attestation: No pre-867 CE written attestation found; urbanized in the late 19th to early 20th century CE around a Sanusi zawiya and French post.
b_faya.etymology_analysis: Oasis in Borkou, northern Chad (later called Faya-Largeau under French colonial rule); unattested in historical sources on or before 867 CE.

b_borkou.first_mention_attestation: Gustav Nachtigal, Saharâ und Sûdân (1879–1881 CE, following his 1869–1875 expedition).
b_borkou.etymology_analysis: Regional choronym for the desert depression between Tibesti and the Chad Basin; first documented in external written accounts by Gustav Nachtigal (1879 CE).

b_koro_toro.first_mention_attestation: No pre-867 CE written attestation found; modern settlement and paleoanthropological locality in southern Borkou, Chad.
b_koro_toro.etymology_analysis: Desert settlement in the Bahr el-Ghazal / southern Borkou region of Chad; unattested in historical sources on or before 867 CE.

b_bahr_el-ghazzal_route.first_mention_attestation: Unattested as a historical settlement name; modern English game-design label for the caravan route along Chad's Bahr el-Ghazal wadi.
b_bahr_el-ghazzal_route.etymology_analysis: Modern English compound combining Arabic Baḥr al-Ghazāl ('sea/river of the gazelle', referring to the dry paleochannel in Chad) with 'Route'.

b_tibesti-south.first_mention_attestation: Unattested as a historical toponym; modern English directional subdivision of the Tibesti Mountains (Tibesti itself first documented by Nachtigal in 1879 CE).
b_tibesti-south.etymology_analysis: Modern English directional compound ('Tibesti-South') based on Tibesti (Kanuri/Teda for 'place where the mountain people [Tubu] live', first documented by Gustav Nachtigal in 1879 CE).

b_tibesti-central.first_mention_attestation: Unattested as a historical toponym; modern English directional subdivision of the Tibesti Mountains (Tibesti itself first documented by Nachtigal in 1879 CE).
b_tibesti-central.etymology_analysis: Modern English directional compound ('Tibesti-Central') based on Tibesti (first documented by Gustav Nachtigal in 1879 CE).

b_bardai.first_mention_attestation: Gustav Nachtigal, Saharâ und Sûdân (1879 CE, following his 1869 visit).
b_bardai.etymology_analysis: From Chadian Arabic barda'i ('cold', referring to the highland climate), known in indigenous Tedaga as Goumodi ('red pass'); first described in detail by Gustav Nachtigal in 1869 (published 1879 CE).

b_tibesti_route.first_mention_attestation: Unattested as a historical settlement name; modern English game-design label for the Tibesti caravan corridor.
b_tibesti_route.etymology_analysis: Modern English compound combining the mountain range name Tibesti with 'Route' to represent a trans-Saharan caravan corridor.
